newsitem.title: CYPRUS: U.S. envoy arrives in Cyprus to defuse tension.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy arrives in Cyprus to defuse tension.

text.p: A U.S. envoy who arrived in Cyprus on Sunday night expressed opposition to the government's planned deployment of Russian missiles on the divided island.

U.S. State Department official Carey Cavanaugh said the Cypriot government's plans to deploy Russian made anti-aircraft missiles "is a step down the wrong path" in efforts to find a solution to the long standing dispute.
He was equally critical of threats made last week by Turkey -- which occupies the northern third of the island -- to retaliate with military action.
"There can be no justification for military action," Cavanaugh, Director of the State Department's South European Department, told reporters on arrival.
"No aggressive action here can be justified in any form," he added.
Turkey has threatened military action to stop the deployment of the S-300 anti-aircraft missiles, which the Cypriot government announced last week it would acquire from Russia.

The Turkish Cypriot administration in the northern part of the island also threatened to move people into Varosha, a now empty tourist resort once mainly owned by Greek Cypriots but now in occupied northern Cyprus.

Cavanaugh, who will attempt to defuse the tension caused on the island over the planned missile deployment, on Monday will hold talks with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
Cavanaugh did not say whether or not he would ask the Cypriot government to scrap the missile purchase.
"I am going to discuss the missile deal and lay out the concerns we have and the problems that it poses for our diplomatic efforts," he said.
"I think it should be understood that that deal in many ways represents a setback to efforts the international community is trying to achieve on Cyprus."
The Cypriot government has refused to back down on the deal, saying the missiles are necessary for defensive purposes in the event of an air raid by Turkey.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded northern Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has some 30,000 troops in the northern third of Cyprus, which has declared a Turkish Cypriot state that is only recognised by Ankara.
Cavanaugh said it was easy to understand the reasons behind the missile purchase, but queried the timing.
"What is less clear is why the decision has to be made now to move forward in this direction. There has been no recent threat by Turkey," he said.
Turkish Chief of Staff Ismail Hakki Karadayi will travel to north Cyprus on Monday for a two-day visit on the invitation of Denktash.
